title: Lesson 4.1: Yield farming, base yield vs emissions
use: Lesson 4.1 page in the Whop course. Hand-written gold-standard script: base yield vs emissions, why emissions APYs fall, mercenary liquidity, and the source material's own 60% APY worked example, as walk-throughs.

scenes.title: Yield farming: base yield vs emissions
scenes.sub: Would you take the risk for what's left, once the printing stops?
scenes.vo: Lesson four point one. Yield farming: base yield versus emissions. By the end, you'll be able to split any farm's advertised A.P.Y. into what's actually earned, and what's simply printed, and answer the one question that actually matters about it.
scenes.cap: Lesson 4.1. Yield farming: base yield vs emissions. By the end, you'll be able to split any farm's advertised APY into what's actually earned, and what's simply printed, and answer the one question that actually matters about it.

scenes.title: What this lesson covers

items.title: Base yield
items.text: Trading fees or borrower interest, from real users

items.title: Emissions
items.text: New tokens printed to attract deposits

items.title: Worked example
items.text: 60% APY, split down to the real number

scenes.vo: Here's the plan. Base yield, what's genuinely earned from real activity. Emissions, what's simply printed and handed out. Mercenary liquidity, the capital that only ever showed up for the printing. And a full worked example, using the source material's own sixty percent A.P.Y. farm, split all the way down to the number that actually matters.

scenes.title: Two sources, one number on the dashboard
scenes.sub: Both can produce the exact same-looking APY.
scenes.vo: Base yield vs. emissions.

scenes.eyebrow: Where a farm's APY actually comes from
scenes.vo: Here's exactly where a farming A.P.Y. splits, underneath that single headline number. Base yield is trading fees, or borrower interest, paid by real users doing real activity, the same kind of yield you'd find in any lending market or A.M.M. Emissions are new tokens, printed directly by the protocol, and handed out specifically to attract deposits it wants right now. Both get added together into the one number the dashboard actually shows you.

scenes.title: Why emissions APYs tend to fall

nodes.label: Reward token price often falls
nodes.sub: As more of it gets printed and sold

nodes.label: Real value falls twice over
nodes.sub: Dilution, plus a falling token price

scenes.vo: Here's the actual mechanism behind why emissions A.P.Y.s tend to fall over time, even when nothing else about the farm changes. More capital arrives, chasing the advertised rate. That capital shares the same fixed pool of reward tokens, so each depositor's individual share shrinks. And separately, as more of the reward token gets printed and sold, its own market price very often declines, shrinking the real value of that share even further, on top of the dilution.

lines: A deliberate cost, paid in the protocol's own token.
Reasonable for bootstrapping. The mistake is treating it as durable.
scenes.sub: A subsidy, correctly labeled, is fine. Mislabeled, it's the whole problem.
scenes.vo: Worth being precise about what emissions actually are, since the word can sound negative when it isn't automatically. Emissions are a cost, deliberately paid in the protocol's own token, to buy deposits faster than organic activity alone would attract them. That can be a completely reasonable strategy, for a protocol genuinely trying to bootstrap early liquidity. The only mistake is treating that printed cost as if it were durable, ordinary yield.

scenes.title: Finding the split yourself
steps: Check trading volume vs TVL, with the fee rate, for base yield
Check the emissions dashboard for reward tokens allocated to that pool
Headline APY minus base yield = the emissions portion
scenes.vo: Here's how to actually find this split yourself, when a farm's own dashboard doesn't show it broken out already. Check the underlying pool's trading volume against its total value locked, since that ratio, combined with the pool's fee rate, gives you a genuine estimate of the base yield. Separately, check the protocol's emissions dashboard or documentation for exactly how many reward tokens are allocated to that specific pool. And treat whatever's left over, once base yield is subtracted from the headline number, as the emissions portion.

scenes.q: What's the test for a farm?
scenes.a: Does the base yield alone justify the risk?
scenes.vo: Quick check. What's the actual test for whether a farm is worth the risk? [[pause 4]] The answer: does the base yield alone, with emissions removed entirely, justify the risk you'd be taking on.

scenes.title: Capital that only ever showed up for the printing
scenes.sub: It leaves the moment the incentives do. Often taking the base yield with it.
scenes.vo: Mercenary liquidity.

scenes.title: The mercenary liquidity cycle

nodes.label: Arrives for the emissions rate
nodes.sub: Not genuine interest in the protocol

nodes.label: Takes base yield with it
nodes.sub: Less real activity, for whoever remains

scenes.vo: Here's the actual sequence mercenary liquidity follows, from arrival to departure. It arrives specifically chasing an attractive emissions rate, not because it has any particular interest in that protocol. It stays for exactly as long as that rate remains attractive relative to alternatives elsewhere. And the moment incentives are reduced, or end, it leaves, often within days, taking a large share of the pool's total liquidity with it as it goes.

lines: Thinner liquidity often means thinner base yield too.
Remaining depositors can lose on both fronts at once.
scenes.sub: The exit doesn't just remove emissions. It can shrink what's left too.
scenes.vo: Worth being precise about the actual damage this does to whoever stays behind, since it isn't just that the emissions disappear. When a large share of a pool's liquidity leaves all at once, trading in that pool often gets thinner and more volatile too, meaning even the genuine, organic base yield can fall for the depositors who remain, on top of losing the emissions entirely.

left.label: Mercenary capital
items: Moves the instant a better rate appears elsewhere

right.label: Base-yield capital
items: Was never there for the emissions
Tends to stay through emissions changes

scenes.vo: Here's the actual difference between capital that's mercenary and capital that isn't, side by side, since not every depositor in a farm behaves the same way. Mercenary capital tracks the emissions rate specifically, and moves the instant a better rate appears anywhere else. Capital that's there for the base yield itself tends to stay through emissions changes, since it was never the reason it showed up in the first place.

scenes.a: Capital that moves on as soon as incentives end.
scenes.vo: Quick check. What is mercenary liquidity, exactly? [[pause 4]] The answer: capital that moves on as soon as incentives end, often taking a large share of the pool's base yield along with it.

scenes.title: A 60% APY farm, split all the way down
scenes.vo: Worked example.

scenes.title: The headline number, split
steps: Already: over 90% of the headline is emissions
scenes.result: A number that's almost entirely printed, not earned
scenes.vo: Here's the farm, exactly as advertised. A dashboard shows sixty percent A.P.Y., total. Split honestly, that's five percent from genuine trading fees, and fifty-five percent paid out in reward tokens, as emissions. Already, before anything else happens, more than ninety percent of that headline number is emissions, not organic activity.

scenes.title: Valuing the reward token realistically (−50% average)
scenes.vo: Now here's what happens once you account for the reward token's actual price, using the source material's own realistic assumption: that it falls fifty percent, on average, across the period you're actually harvesting and selling it. Fifty-five percent of emissions, valued at half price, is worth about twenty-seven and a half percent, not the full fifty-five. Add that back to the five percent in genuine fees, and the real return comes to about thirty-two and a half percent.

right.label: Emissions removed entirely
items: What's left once the subsidy is gone

scenes.vo: And here's the actual question this whole exercise exists to answer, laid out side by side. With emissions included, even realistically discounted, the farm still shows an attractive thirty-two and a half percent. But strip emissions out completely, and account for nothing except genuine, durable activity, and you're left with exactly five percent.

lines: Would you take this protocol's risk for 5%?
Not the headline. Not the realistic number either.
scenes.sub: That's the real question. Everything else is the subsidy talking.
scenes.vo: Here's the one question this entire worked example exists to make you ask, every single time, before entering any farm. Would you take on this specific protocol's risk, its smart contract risk, its impermanent loss, its gas costs, for five percent? Not for the sixty percent headline. Not even for the thirty-two and a half percent realistic number. For the five percent that's actually durable.

scenes.title: The same farm, at five different price assumptions
scenes.sub: One assumption drives almost the entire result.
scenes.vo: How sensitive is that number, really?

scenes.title: Real return vs. reward-token price decline
scenes.vo: Here's the exact same farm, run across five different assumptions for how far the reward token actually falls, from a full recovery to a total collapse. If the reward token doesn't fall at all, the real return is the full sixty percent headline. At a twenty-five percent decline, it's about forty-six percent. At the source material's own fifty percent assumption, thirty-two and a half. At seventy-five percent, under nineteen. And if the reward token falls to zero, all that's left is the five percent in genuine fees.

scenes.kicker: What the straight line tells you
lines: The whole result rides on one assumption.
Guess too small a decline, and you overestimate by that same margin.
scenes.sub: This is why 'realistic, not best-case' matters so much.
scenes.vo: Notice how this line is almost perfectly straight, which tells you something important: the entire result rides on a single assumption, how much the reward token actually falls, and that assumption drives the outcome almost one-for-one. Guess a smaller decline than what actually happens, and you've overestimated your real return by roughly that same margin.

scenes.title: Estimating the decline yourself
steps: Check the reward token's price during past emissions periods
Check the emission schedule — faster printing, faster dilution
When unsure, default to the more conservative estimate
scenes.result: A farm that clears the conservative bar clears the optimistic one too
scenes.vo: Here's how to actually estimate that decline yourself, for a real farm, instead of guessing. Pull up the reward token's own price chart, and look specifically at how it's behaved during past emissions periods, not just its all-time high. Check the emission schedule itself, since a faster printing rate tends to mean faster dilution. And when genuinely unsure, default to the more conservative estimate, since a farm that clears that bar clears the optimistic one too.

scenes.a: More capital shares the rewards, and the reward token's price often declines.
scenes.vo: Quick check. Why do emissions A.P.Y.s tend to fall over time? [[pause 4]] The answer: more capital arrives to share the same reward pool, and the reward token's own price often declines as more of it gets printed and sold.

scenes.title: Decide this before you enter, not during
scenes.sub: A rule set in advance beats a decision made while watching the price move.
scenes.vo: Setting your harvest schedule.

scenes.kicker: Why this gets decided in advance
lines: A fixed schedule removes the in-the-moment temptation to hold.
Hoping for a recovery isn't a plan; it's the way you lose the real return.
scenes.sub: Decide the rule once. Then just follow it.
scenes.vo: Worth deciding this specific detail before you ever deposit, not while you're already watching the reward token's price move in real time. A fixed schedule, say harvesting and converting to a stablecoin on a set day each week, removes the temptation to hold reward tokens hoping for a recovery that the earlier chart just showed you isn't the way to bet.

scenes.title: Your checklist
steps: APY split into base yield vs incentives
Reward token valued at a realistic, falling price
scenes.vo: Here's your checklist. Do it before entering any farm, not after. Split the advertised A.P.Y. into base yield versus incentives, explicitly, using the protocol's own numbers. Value the reward token at a realistic price, one that assumes it falls, not its current, best-case price. And set your harvest-and-sell schedule in advance, rather than deciding it emotionally, in the moment, while watching the token's price move.

scenes.title: Just to prove this isn't a one-off calculation
scenes.sub: Purely illustrative, to show the method transfers.
scenes.vo: The same method, a different farm.

scenes.title: A different farm, same method (illustrative)
scenes.vo: Here's the same method, applied to a completely different, purely illustrative farm, just to show it's a repeatable habit, not a one-off calculation tied to that specific sixty percent example. Say a farm shows eighty percent A.P.Y.: ten percent fees, seventy percent emissions. At the same realistic fifty percent decline assumption, that's forty-five percent real return, and just ten percent with emissions removed entirely. Same method. Same honest question, on a completely different number.

scenes.title: Recap
items: Base yield: real activity. Emissions: printed, not durable
Emissions APYs fall through dilution and falling token price
Mercenary liquidity leaves when incentives end — often taking base yield with it
The real question: what's left once emissions are removed entirely?
scenes.vo: Let's recap. Base yield comes from real activity: fees and borrower interest. Emissions are printed tokens, a deliberate cost, not durable yield. Emissions A.P.Y.s tend to fall, through dilution and falling token price, together. Mercenary liquidity arrives for the emissions and leaves the moment they end, often taking base yield with it. And the real question is never the headline number: it's what's left once emissions are gone entirely.
Before entering any farm, split its APY, value the reward token realistically, and ask whether the base yield alone is worth the risk. Next up, Lesson four point two: native staking.
